country.comment: The empirical village-level infrastructure/epidemiological analysis and statutory/policy review focus on Brazil (specifically the state of Tocantins in the Brazilian Legal Amazon). The accompanying PRISMA systematic literature review component applied no geographic restrictions and discusses international literature (including Canada, Australia, the United States and New Zealand).

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive administrative statistics only; although PDF p. 4 states chi-square tests and t-tests (p<0.05) would be used where applicable, no inferential test statistics, confidence intervals or p-values are reported in the paper. Minor internal discrepancies exist in the printed text/tables: Table 3 sums to 161 villages (17 + 93 + 51) and 11,688 people, whereas text on p. 6 and Table 4 sum to 160 villages (17 + 92 + 51); text on p. 6 states 51 ADD cases in the group without WSS/SM, whereas Table 4 reports 131 ADD cases in that group; and Abstract/Conclusion state 30% of the Indigenous population lacks treated water whereas 51/160 villages is 31.8% and 1,737/11,688 people in Table 3 is 14.9%.
effect_estimate.value: Across 160 Indigenous villages in DSEI-Tocantins (11,908 Indigenous residents per SIASI 2019; 11,688 residents across 161 villages in Table 3), only 17 villages (10.6%; 3,037 residents) have both a Water Supply System (WSS) and domestic Sanitary Modules (SM), 93 villages (58%; 6,914 residents) have WSS/water treatment without SM, and 51 villages (31.8%; 1,737 residents; summarized in Abstract/Conclusion as 10% of villages having both systems and 30% of the Indigenous population lacking treated water) lack both WSS and SM, violating PNASPI mandates. In 2017, acute diarrheal disease (ADD) incidence was 360 cases among 3,037 residents with WSS and SM (11.85%), 933 cases among 6,914 residents with WSS only (13.49%), and 131 cases in Table 4 (reported as 51 cases in text on p. 6, attributed to under-notification) among 1,737 residents without WSS and SM.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <=2 by non-experimental/non-quasi-experimental design. Rated 1 because the study descriptively documents severe service coverage deficits under the PNASPI/SESAI statutory regime using official secondary administrative data (Tables 3-4) alongside a legislative review and literature synthesis, but does not directly observe village-level administrative processes or test statistical associations with institutional variables in Tocantins (claims regarding weak social control, standardized SESAI management and resource allocation rely on secondary literature).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Doctrinal-empirical / legal-institutional policy implementation study combining a review of 10 Brazilian statutes/decrees/ordinances (PNASPI, Law 11,445/2007, Law 14,026/2020, Ordinance 888/2021), a PRISMA systematic review (44 studies), and descriptive official administrative data from 160 Indigenous villages (SESAI/SIASI). Fits Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework best because it goes beyond a secondary systematic review (AMSTAR 2) by analyzing village-level administrative data, yet reports neither primary qualitative fieldwork (MMAT/CASP) nor analytical cross-sectional regression/hypothesis testing (JBI).

sample_size.comment: Paper combines three data components: (1) official SESAI/SIASI administrative and epidemiological data on 160 Indigenous villages in DSEI-Tocantins (p. 6 cites 11,908 individuals across 160 villages from SIASI 2019; Table 3 sums to 11,688 individuals and 161 villages across 5 ethnic rows; Table 4 sums to 11,688 individuals and 160 villages); (2) PRISMA systematic review of 44 included peer-reviewed studies (from 423 Scopus records identified, 389 screened, 91 full texts assessed); and (3) policy/legislative review of 10 federal legal/regulatory instruments in Table 2.

study_design.comment: Although PDF p. 4 mentions primary data collection and chi-square/t-tests where applicable, the actual operationalized empirical component extracts secondary administrative data from SESAI/SIASI reports (Brasil, 2019) and presents descriptive frequencies/percentages only (Tables 3-4), alongside a PRISMA systematic review of Scopus literature and a doctrinal review of Brazilian laws and health/sanitation ordinances.
study_design.value: Multi-component legal-empirical study combining a PRISMA systematic literature review, doctrinal/policy review of Brazilian legislation, and descriptive cross-sectional analysis of secondary official administrative/epidemiological data (SESAI/SIASI) on Indigenous villages
